fields.title: The Letter to the Colossians
fields.subtitle: Pros Kolossaeis, “To the Colossians”
fields.description: Paul’s letter from prison to a small church in the Lycus valley that he had never visited, which was being offered something more than Christ: a deeper philosophy, strict rules about food and festivals, visions and the worship of angels. His answer is Christ himself: “The Son is the image of the unseen God,” through whom and for whom everything was created, in whom all things are held together, and in whom all the fullness of God dwells bodily. So the Colossians need nothing more. Raised with Christ, they are to seek what is above, put on the new self and, over all, love, and live as a household in the Lord, where Christ is everything, and he is in all. Carried by Tychicus with Onesimus, alongside the letter to Philemon. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Colossians?
qa.answer: The twelfth book of the New Testament, a letter of the apostle Paul and Timothy to the church at Colossae, a town in the Lycus valley in what is now western Turkey. Paul had never visited it; the gospel reached it through Epaphras, one of its own (1:7; 4:12). The letter answers teachers who were offering the Colossians something beyond Christ, by setting out who Christ is, the image of the unseen God and the one in whom all God’s fullness dwells, and what it means to live raised with him.

qa.question: Who wrote Colossians, and when?
qa.answer: The letter comes from Paul and Timothy, and Paul signs it in his own hand (4:18). It is closely tied to Philemon: the same companions are with Paul, and Onesimus travels with Tychicus to Colossae (4:7–9). Most readers date both letters to Paul’s imprisonment, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, though some prefer Ephesus. Some scholars think a disciple wrote Colossians in Paul’s name, pointing to its style and its vision of Christ; others hold that its links with Philemon make Paul’s authorship the simplest explanation.

qa.question: What was the false teaching at Colossae?
qa.answer: No one knows exactly, because Paul never describes it in full. He warns against a philosophy that follows human tradition and the elemental forces of the world (2:8), and mentions rules about food and drink, festivals, new moons and the sabbath, self-humbling, the worship of angels, visions, and the slogan “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” (2:16–23). Many think it mixed Jewish practice with mystical or local religion. Paul’s answer is that in Christ believers have been made full (2:10), so they need nothing more.

qa.question: Does “firstborn” in Colossians 1:15 mean that Christ was created?
qa.answer: Paul calls the Son “the firstborn who stands above all creation”, and goes straight on to say that everything in heaven and on earth was created in him, through him and for him, and that in him all things are held together (1:16–17). The word speaks of rank, the place of the heir, not of being the first thing made. In the fourth century the followers of Arius argued otherwise, and Athanasius answered from the passage itself: if all creation came to be through the Son and holds together in him, he cannot be one of the things he holds together. The churches have followed him.

qa.question: What does “Christ in you, the hope of glory” mean in Colossians 1:27?
qa.answer: Paul speaks of a mystery kept hidden through all past ages and now revealed: that among the Gentiles, of all people, Christ himself lives in those who believe, and that his presence is the promise of the glory still to come. It is his answer to teachers who said the Colossians needed something more, a deeper philosophy, stricter rules, visions or the help of angels. In Christ all the fullness of God dwells, and in him they have been made full (2:9–10). Their life now lies hidden with Christ in God, and when he is revealed they will be revealed with him in glory (3:3–4).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The Son is the image of the unseen God, the firstborn who stands above all creation. For in him everything in heaven and on earth was created, the seen and the unseen, whether thrones or dominions, rulers or authorities. Everything has been created through him and for him. He exists before all things, and all things are held together in him. He is also the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the first to be born from among the dead, so that he would come to hold first place in everything. For God in all his fullness was pleased to dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross: all things through him, on earth and in heaven alike.

— Colossians 1:15–20

Colossians is a short letter with the largest possible subject. It was written to a small church in a country town that Paul had never visited, and it was carried there by a friend named Tychicus, who travelled with a slave named Onesimus. Yet in its first chapter it speaks of Christ as the one through whom everything in heaven and on earth was created, in whom all things are held together, and through whom God will reconcile all things to himself.

Paul writes that way because the church at Colossae was being told it needed something more than Christ: a deeper philosophy, stricter rules, visions, the help of angels. His answer fills four chapters and can be put in one line from the third: “Christ is everything, and he is in all.”

Colossae and its church

Colossae lay inland from Ephesus, in the valley of the river Lycus, within fifteen miles of two larger cities, Laodicea and Hierapolis. It had been an important town once, on the road from the coast to the east, but by Paul’s day it was overshadowed by its neighbours. Laodicea, rich and confident, is the church that Revelation later calls lukewarm (Revelation 3:14–22).

Paul did not found the church. He speaks of the readers as among “everyone who has never met me in person” (2:1). The gospel came to them through Epaphras, one of their own: “You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant” (1:7). Most likely Epaphras heard it during the years Paul spent in Ephesus, when, as Acts says, all the people of the province of Asia heard the word of the Lord (Acts 19:10). Now Epaphras is with Paul, and the news he has brought is mixed: the church is growing in faith and love, but it is being unsettled by teachers who offer it something more.

Who wrote it

The letter comes from Paul and Timothy (1:1), and Paul signs it in his own hand at the end, adding, “Remember that I am in chains” (4:18). Its closest companion is the little letter to Philemon. The same people are with Paul in both, Timothy, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke and Demas; Archippus is named in both; and Onesimus, the subject of Philemon, travels with Tychicus to Colossae (4:9). Most readers have taken the two as written and sent together, from prison, probably in Rome around AD 60–62, though some place them in an earlier imprisonment at Ephesus.

Some scholars think Colossians was written in Paul’s name by one of his disciples, pointing to differences of style and to its vision of Christ as head of the whole church and of the universe. Others answer that a new problem called for new words, and that the letter’s ties to Philemon, which almost everyone accepts as Paul’s, make his authorship the simplest explanation. The church has always read it as his.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: Christ above all. Thanksgiving and prayer for the Colossians; the great passage on the Son, the image of the unseen God; and Paul’s own work, to make known “Christ in you, the hope of glory.”
  • Chapter 2: Christ is enough. A warning against an empty philosophy, and the answer to it: in Christ all the fullness of God dwells, and in him you have been made full.
  • Chapters 3–4: life hidden with Christ. Setting the mind on what is above; the old self and the new; a household in the Lord; prayer, wise speech and a long list of friends.

The image of the unseen God

Paul opens, as he usually does, with thanks and prayer. Then, almost without a pause, he begins to speak of the Son, in the lines that open this introduction. Many readers think they were an early Christian hymn, and they fall into two halves. In the first, the Son is Lord of creation: everything was made in him, through him and for him, and in him all things are held together. In the second, he is Lord of the new creation: the head of the church, the first to be born from among the dead, the one through whom God makes peace “by the blood of his cross.”

No passage in Paul says more about who Christ is. The Son is not one heavenly power among many, to be added to the others. Every power in the universe, “whether thrones or dominions, rulers or authorities,” was made through him and for him. In the fourth century the followers of Arius pointed to the word “firstborn” to argue that the Son was the first of God’s creatures, and Athanasius answered them from the passage itself: if all creation came to be through the Son and holds together in him, how can he be one of the things that hold together in him?

Paul then tells his readers what this means for them. They were once estranged from God; now they have been reconciled by Christ’s death. And the mystery hidden for ages has been revealed, among Gentiles of all people: “Christ in you, the hope of glory.” Paul says that in his own sufferings he is “completing what is still lacking in Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of his body, the church” (1:24). Readers of every tradition agree that he cannot mean Christ’s saving death was not enough; most take him to mean the sufferings that Christ’s people must still bear, which Christ counts as his own.

The philosophy and the fullness

In chapter 2 Paul turns to the danger. He warns against “philosophy that is empty deceit,” which follows human tradition and “the elemental forces of the world,” not Christ. He mentions food and drink, festivals, new moons and the sabbath; self-humbling and “the worship of angels”; visions; and rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch.”

No one is quite sure what the Colossian teaching was, since Paul never sets it out. Some think it was a form of Jewish mysticism, in which strict fasting and observance prepared the soul for visions of the angels worshipping in heaven; others, a blend of Jewish practice and local folk religion. Paul’s answer does not depend on the details:

For all the fullness of God’s own being dwells in him bodily, and in him you have been made full. He is the head over every ruler and authority. In him you were also circumcised, with a circumcision no hand performed: the old life that the flesh ruled was stripped off you, in the circumcision that Christ gives. You were buried with him in baptism, and in baptism you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead.

— Colossians 2:9–12

The Colossians need nothing more, because in Christ they have everything. God has forgiven all their trespasses, wiped out the bond of debt that stood against them, “nailing it to the cross,” and led the hostile powers captive in his victory procession. Rules about food and festivals are “a shadow of what was coming; the substance is Christ.” And the hard regulations of self-denial, for all their look of wisdom, are worth nothing for holding back the indulgence of the flesh.

Raised with Christ

What does work, then? Not rules, but a new life:

You have been raised with Christ, then. So seek what is above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. Fix your thoughts on what is above, not on what is on earth. For you died, and the life you now have lies hidden with Christ in God. Christ is your life. When he is revealed, you too will be revealed with him in glory.

— Colossians 3:1–4

From that, everything else follows. The old ways are put to death and taken off like old clothes, and the new self is put on, “being made new, growing in knowledge, in the image of its Creator.” In this new humanity it no longer counts whether one is Greek or Jew, slave or free. Believers are to put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, and to forgive as the Lord has forgiven them. “Over all of these put on love.” Christ’s peace is to settle their disputes, his word is to make its home among them richly, and everything they say and do is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks.

A household in the Lord

Like Ephesians, Colossians then speaks to each member of a household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (3:18–4:1). Christians apply these words to marriage today in different ways, and the words to slaves belong to a world where slavery was taken for granted. But it is striking how much more Paul says to slaves than to anyone else, telling them that they will receive an inheritance from the Lord and that it is the Lord Christ they serve. And he tells masters to give their slaves “what is right and fair,” because they too have a Master in heaven. These words were read aloud in a church where Onesimus, a slave returning to his master, now sat as “our faithful and dear brother, who is one of your own.”

A circle of friends

The letter ends with prayer, with a word about speech that is gracious and “seasoned with salt”, and with greetings that let us glimpse the people around Paul. Aristarchus, his fellow prisoner. Mark, “the cousin of Barnabas,” once the cause of a quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39), now commended. “Our dear friend Luke, the doctor.” Epaphras, still wrestling in prayer for his home church. And Nympha, with the church that meets in her house. The Colossians are to swap letters with Laodicea (4:16); the letter from Laodicea has not survived, unless, as some think, it is the one we call Ephesians.

How to read Colossians

Read it alongside Philemon, which was carried on the same journey, and alongside Ephesians, which shares so much of its wording. Read it first straight through, in a quarter of an hour, and then slowly.

Notice the words “all” and “fullness”, which keep returning, and the phrases “in him” and “with him”: buried with him, raised with him, hidden with him, revealed with him. Notice how Paul answers every offer of something more with Christ himself. And notice how a letter that begins with the creation of the universe ends with a list of ordinary people, greeted by name.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Colossians are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Firstborn.” In 1:15 the translation reads “the firstborn who stands above all creation,” making clear that the word is about rank, the place of the heir, and not about the Son being the first thing created.

“Elemental forces.” Paul’s phrase in 2:8 and 2:20 is hard to pin down. It may mean the basic principles of religion, or the powers thought to rule the world. The translation says “the elemental forces of the world,” which leaves room for both.

“The umpire in your hearts.” In 3:15 Paul uses a word from the games, for the judge who settles a contest, and the translation keeps the picture: “Let the peace that Christ gives be the umpire in your hearts.”

Places where manuscripts differ. In 1:14 it reads, with the oldest manuscripts, “In him we have redemption, which is the forgiveness of our sins”; some later manuscripts add “through his blood”, from Ephesians 1:7. And in 4:15 it reads Nympha, a woman, and “the church that meets in her house”; other manuscripts have a man’s name.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Colossians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

1From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and from Timothy our brother, 2to God’s holy people in Colossae, the faithful brothers and sisters in Christ. Grace and peace to you from God our Father.

Thanks for their faith and love

3Every time we pray for you, we give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, 4because we have heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you have for all God’s holy people. 5That faith and love spring from the hope kept safe for you in heaven, the hope you first heard about in the message of truth, the gospel 6that has reached you. All over the world this gospel is bearing fruit and growing, and it has done the same among you from the day you heard it and came to know God’s grace in all its truth. 7You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who serves Christ faithfully on our behalf. 8He is also the one who told us about your love in the Spirit.

Paul’s prayer, and the Son above all creation

9That is why, from the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will, with all the wisdom and understanding the Spirit gives, 10so that you may live in a way worthy of the Lord and please him in every way, bearing fruit in every kind of good work and growing in the knowledge of God. 11We ask that you be made strong with all power by his glorious might, so that you may endure everything with patience and joy, 12and give thanks to the Father, who has made you fit to share in the inheritance of God’s holy people in the light. 13He has rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves. 14In him we have redemption, which is the forgiveness of our sins. 15The Son is the image of the unseen God, the firstborn who stands above all creation. 16For in him everything in heaven and on earth was created, the seen and the unseen, whether thrones or dominions, rulers or authorities. Everything has been created through him and for him. 17He exists before all things, and all things are held together in him. 18He is also the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, the first to be born from among the dead, so that he would come to hold first place in everything. 19For God in all his fullness was pleased to dwell in him, 20and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross: all things through him, on earth and in heaven alike. 21Once you were estranged from God, hostile to him in your thinking, as your evil deeds showed. 22But now you have been reconciled by Christ’s death in his physical body, so that God may bring you into his presence holy, without blemish, and free from any charge, 23provided that you stay in the faith, firm on your foundation and steady, not drifting away from the hope held out in the gospel you heard. This gospel has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and I, Paul, have become its servant.

Paul toils to make the mystery known

24Now I am glad to suffer for your sake. In my own body I am completing what is still lacking in Christ’s afflictions, for the sake of his body, the church. 25I became its servant by the task God gave me for your benefit: to make the word of God fully known, 26the mystery that was kept hidden through all past ages and generations but has now been revealed to his holy people. 27God chose to make known to them how rich and glorious this mystery is among the Gentiles. The mystery is this: Christ in you, the hope of glory. 28Christ is the one we proclaim. We warn every person and teach every person with all wisdom, so that we may bring every person before God mature in Christ. 29This is the goal I toil for, struggling by his energy, which is powerfully at work in me.
fields.summary: Paul thanks God for the Colossians’ faith and love and prays that they may know God’s will. The Son is the image of the invisible God, above all creation and head of the church, and Paul toils to make the mystery known.

fields.title: Colossians 2
fields.body_html:
1I want you to know how hard I am struggling for you, for those in Laodicea, and for everyone who has never met me in person. 2My aim is that their hearts may be encouraged as they are joined together in love, and that they may have all the riches of understanding held with full confidence, so that they know God’s mystery, which is Christ himself. 3In him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden. 4I tell you this so that no one will lead you astray with arguments that only sound convincing. 5I may be far away in body, but in spirit I am there with you. I am glad as I see your orderly life and the solid strength of your faith in Christ.

Made full in Christ

6You have received Christ Jesus as Lord. So let your whole life be lived in him, 7with roots sunk deep in him, built up in him, made strong in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thanks to God.

8Watch out, so that no one carries you off like captives by means of philosophy that is empty deceit. It follows human tradition and the elemental forces of the world, not Christ. 9For all the fullness of God’s own being dwells in him bodily, 10and in him you have been made full. He is the head over every ruler and authority. 11In him you were also circumcised, with a circumcision no hand performed: the old life that the flesh ruled was stripped off you, in the circumcision that Christ gives. 12You were buried with him in baptism, and in baptism you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead. 13You were dead in your trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, but God made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our trespasses. 14He wiped out the bond of debt, with its decrees, that was written against us and stood opposed to us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. 15He disarmed the rulers and authorities and exposed them to public disgrace, leading them as captives in his victory procession by the cross.

Rules that are only a shadow

16So no one should sit in judgment on you over food and drink, or over keeping a festival, a new moon or the sabbath. 17These things are a shadow of what was coming; the substance is Christ. 18Do not let anyone rob you of the prize: someone who delights in self-humbling and the worship of angels, who takes his stand on the visions he has seen and is puffed up for nothing by a mind set on the flesh. 19Such a person has lost hold of the head, Christ. From him the whole body, supplied and held together by its joints and ligaments, grows with the growth God gives.

20Since you died with Christ and were set free from the elemental forces of the world, why do you live as though you still belonged to the world? Why submit to rules like 21“Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch”? 22All these things are meant to be used up and to perish. Such rules come from human commands and teachings. 23Rules like these have the look of wisdom, with their worship that people choose for themselves, their self-humbling and their severe treatment of the body. Yet they are worth nothing for holding back the indulgence of the flesh.
fields.summary: Believers have been made full in Jesus and must not be taken captive by empty philosophy. Rules about food and festivals are only a shadow, and the reality belongs to Jesus.

fields.title: Colossians 3
fields.body_html:
Raised with Christ

1You have been raised with Christ, then. So seek what is above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. 2Fix your thoughts on what is above, not on what is on earth. 3For you died, and the life you now have lies hidden with Christ in God. 4Christ is your life. When he is revealed, you too will be revealed with him in glory.

Put to death what belongs to the earth

5So put to death whatever in you belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, lustful passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry. 6Because of these things the wrath of God is coming on those who disobey. 7You too once lived among such people, when your life was given over to these things. 8But now put all these away, every one: anger, bursts of temper, malice, slander, and foul words from your mouths. 9Do not lie to one another. You have stripped off the old self and its ways 10and have put on the new self, which is being made new, growing in knowledge, in the image of its Creator. 11In this new humanity it no longer counts whether one is Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free. Christ is everything, and he is in all.

Clothed in love

12You are God’s chosen people, holy and loved by him. So put on, like clothing, a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. 13Be patient with one another’s faults, and when someone has a grievance against another, forgive. The Lord has forgiven you freely; you must do the same. 14Over all of these put on love, which binds everything together and makes it complete. 15Let the peace that Christ gives be the umpire in your hearts. You were called to this peace as members of one body. And be thankful. 16Let the word of Christ make its home among you richly, in all wisdom. Teach and warn one another with psalms, hymns and Spirit-given songs, and sing to God, thankful from the heart. 17In everything you say and everything you do, act in the name of the Lord Jesus, and through him give thanks to God the Father.

Life in the household

18Wives, submit to your husbands; this is fitting for those who belong to the Lord. 19Husbands, love your wives and never turn harsh or bitter against them.

20Children, do what your parents tell you in everything, for that is what is pleasing in the Lord. 21Fathers, do not keep provoking your children, or they will lose heart. 22Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything. Do not work only while they are watching, to win their favor, but with an undivided heart, out of reverence for the Lord. 23Whatever you are doing, put your whole self into the work, as for the Lord and not for people, 24knowing that you will receive from the Lord the inheritance as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you serve as slaves. 25Anyone who does wrong will be repaid for that wrong, and there is no favoritism with the Lord.
fields.summary: Raised with Jesus, believers are to set their minds on things above and put to death what belongs to the earth. They are to be clothed in love, let peace rule in their hearts, and live as households that honor the Lord.

fields.title: Colossians 4
fields.body_html:
1Masters, give your slaves what is right and fair, because you know that you too have a Master in heaven.

Pray, and live wisely with outsiders

2Keep on praying, and stay alert as you pray, giving thanks. 3Pray for us too, that God will open a door for our message, so that we can tell the mystery of Christ, which is why I am in chains. 4Pray that I may make it clear, as I ought to.

5Live wisely with those outside the church, making the most of every opportunity. 6Let your conversation always be gracious and seasoned with salt, so that you know how to answer each person.

News and greetings

7Tychicus will tell you all my news. He is a dear brother, a faithful servant and a fellow slave in the Lord. 8I am sending him to you for this very reason, so that you may know how we are and so that he may encourage your hearts. 9He is coming with Onesimus, our faithful and dear brother, who is one of your own. They will tell you everything that is happening here.

10Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, sends you greetings, and so does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas. You have had instructions about him: if he comes to you, make him welcome. 11Jesus who is called Justus greets you too. Of all the Jewish believers, these are the only ones working with me for the kingdom of God, and they have been a great comfort to me. 12Epaphras, one of your own and a servant of Christ, sends you greetings. He always wrestles for you in his prayers, asking that you will stand firm, mature and fully sure of everything God wills. 13I can vouch for him that he works hard for you and for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis. 14Our dear friend Luke, the doctor, sends you greetings, and so does Demas. 15Give my greetings to the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church that meets in her house. 16When this letter has been read to you, see that it is also read in the church at Laodicea, and that you in turn read the letter that comes from Laodicea. 17And tell Archippus, “Make sure you carry out fully the ministry you received in the Lord.”

18I, Paul, write this greeting in my own hand. Remember that I am in chains. Grace be with you.
fields.summary: Paul asks for prayer and urges them to live wisely with outsiders. He sends news through Tychicus and Onesimus and greetings from his companions.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
I, Paul, write this greeting in my own hand. Remember that I am in chains. Grace be with you.

— Colossians 4:18

At the end of the letter Paul takes the pen from his secretary and writes three short sentences of his own. After the soaring lines about the Son through whom all things were made, the last thing the Colossians see is a prisoner’s handwriting, and a request not to forget his chains. It is a fitting close. The Lord of all creation is known in this letter by people in very ordinary places: a country town, a house church, a prison cell.

The question the letter leaves

Colossians asks whether Christ is enough. The teachers at Colossae did not deny Christ; they simply offered more. A deeper wisdom, a stricter discipline, a higher experience, a way to the angels. Every age has its own version of that offer, and it is always attractive, because it promises progress and gives people something to do.

Paul’s answer is not that wisdom, discipline and experience are bad. It is that they are found in Christ, or not at all. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. In him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and in him believers have been made full. To look for something beyond him is not to go deeper but to lose hold of the head. The question the letter leaves is whether we will let Christ be everything, or go on looking for something more.

Where the letter points

It points upward. Those who have been raised with Christ are to seek what is above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God, and to fix their thoughts there. Their life is hidden with him, and when he is revealed they will be revealed with him in glory.

And it points to the church as a new kind of household. Greek and Jew, slave and free, sit together under one Master. A slave who had left Colossae under a cloud comes home as a faithful and dear brother. The letter is to be read aloud, then passed to Laodicea. Christ is not only above all things; he is in all, and he makes a people.

Where to go from here

Colossians has always drawn preachers to its picture of Christ, and many of their sermons and books are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On Christ above all (chapter 1). Athanasius’s Against the Arians, whose second Discourse, in the chapter “Our Lord Not Said to Be Created”, answers those who took “firstborn” in 1:15 to make the Son a creature; A. B. Simpson’s Himself (1:27); and George MacDonald’s “The Inheritance” (1:12), in his Unspoken Sermons.
  • On Christ as enough (chapter 2). Andrew Murray’s Abide in Christ, whose chapter “As You Came to Him, by Faith” is on 2:6–7; and Charles H. Spurgeon’s “Complete in Christ” (2:10), in The Saint and His Saviour.
  • On Christ as everything (3:11). Two sermons on the same three words: J. C. Ryle’s Christ Is All and Dwight L. Moody’s Christ All in All.
  • On the hidden life (chapter 3). Andrew Murray’s “Christ Our Life” (3:4), in The Master’s Indwelling, and “Who Are You?” (3:2–3), in The Inner Chamber; and John Owen’s The Mortification of Sin in Believers, which sets out the duty of 3:5, putting sin to death, beside Romans 8:13.
  • On Paul’s friends (chapter 4). Devoted to Prayer, whose chapter “Always Wrestling in Prayer” is about Epaphras (4:12); and J. C. Ryle’s “Luke, the Beloved Physician” (4:14), in The Upper Room.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Colossians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read Colossians again, together with Philemon, and to hear them as the first hearers did, on the day Tychicus and Onesimus arrived. And then to take Paul’s plainest command as your own:

You have received Christ Jesus as Lord. So let your whole life be lived in him, with roots sunk deep in him, built up in him, made strong in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thanks to God.

— Colossians 2:6–7
